en: The Preface to the *Vajra Needle* is the standard for the contemplation of the Perfect and Real Teaching (*yuan-shi jiao-guan*),

an esoteric treatise that causes the multitude of deluded beings to remove the cataracts of ignorance from their eyes and perceive the fingertip of Buddha-nature. Indeed, among all the teachings of the Mahāyāna...

In the propagation of this school within China, nothing surpasses the ultimate proclamation at the Twin Śāla Trees; yet its texts are so vast and sprawling that they extend into peripheral areas and incorporate provisional teachings.
Consequently, those who study it may find themselves obstructed by the principle of mutual fusion or lingering in the realm of partiality and dogmatism—is this not a grave error?
The Venerable Jingxi felt such profound compassion for this situation that he once entrusted his message to a dream.

I have circulated this work among country guests for thorough investigation; it is exhaustive and complete. Within it, there are places where the instructions are repeated with great earnestness, yet the underlying principles and phrasing are so densely interwoven that they are difficult to discern.

Now that the *Kuang* (Expanded) and *Siji* (Private Record) by [Master] Shanyuan have been published, with their sections clearly divided and their meanings explained with concise precision, those parts that were previously obscure have become as clear as the open sky. However, the old editions contain many errors and omissions, which hinder the reading.
I was grieved by this. The student Biancai of Zhangfu, during the course of our discussions, collated, supplemented, and harmonized these treatises into a single volume for circulation in the world.
If people of the world can employ it, then the realization of the pervasive nature of all teachings and contemplations will perhaps not be difficult.
Once the carving of the blocks was completed, he requested a preface from me. Having an old connection with him, I could not firmly refuse; thus, I comply.
I have recorded this with my brush in sympathetic joy to mark the passage of time.

Written on the first full moon of the first month of spring in the second year of Bunpō, the year of Yichou (1805), by the former Chief Administrator Tan’kū, who was granted the purple robe, at Zampuku-en in the east of Lake Biwa. Recorded by Ōtei Rui.
General Principles: 1. Several versions of this treatise have been circulated, each with slight variations. I have now selected the superior readings and followed them. 2.

Regarding my private notes on the *Shan-jia lun-zhu* (Commentary on the Treatise by the Mountain School), there are mutual discrepancies between various editions. Where one edition is correct and another is not, I have relied upon the former.
Regarding corrections where the meaning is ambiguous, I have marked both versions above; where both versions are erroneous, I have dared to rectify them according to the underlying meaning.
In the *Lunji* (Commentary on the Treatise), many cited passages are quoted by way of their general sense (*yiqi*), yet where the meaning remains unintelligible, I have relied upon...
This text has been revised.

Among the categories of this private record, there are occasional omissions; these have been supplemented by drawing from the works of Master Sik of Seongam or from what I myself have previously heard.
To distinguish these additions, a △ is placed above and a ﹂ is placed below them.
A private note on one treatise states: "The annotated version of the *Jin'gangbei lun* (The Diamond Scalpel) calls it the *Jin'gangbei lun*, while all others simply call it the *Jin'gangbei*.

I follow the annotated version because the term 'scalpel' (*bei*) implies partiality and expedient means; the word 'diamond' (*jin'gang*) is added to signify its capacity to resolve fragmented doubts."
One commentary does not include a title for the author; rather, it takes the first six characters of the work as the author’s title.
Following this approach and omitting a separate section for the author’s title is indeed appropriate.
The preface concludes here.
*Vajrasamādhi-śāstra Private Notes: Compiled Edition*, Volume One.
Composed by the Tiantai Śramaṇa, the Great Master Jingxi;
recorded by his disciple, Dharma Master Mingkuang.
The Zhang Prefecture Collection of the Realm of the Sun; by the Śramaṇa Biancai.
This is divided into two parts: first, the title; second, the entry into the text for explanation. Regarding the first [the title], there are again two parts: first, the title itself.
The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* explains that the term "Golden Scalpel" refers to the eighth chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the "Tathāgata-gotra-parivarta. Therein, Kāśyapa asks the Buddha:
"Why is the Buddha-nature so difficult to see and so difficult to enter? The Buddha replies: "It is like a hundred blind men who, for the sake of treating their eyes, go to a skilled physician."
The skilled physician immediately used a golden probe to clear away the cataract from his eye and pointed with one finger, asking, "Do you see?
He replied, "I do not see. The physician again pointed with two fingers and then three fingers, asking each time, "Do you see? To which he replied, "I see a little. Zhan’an (Zhiyi) said:

"Pointing with one finger is like the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), hence he says he does not see; pointing with three fingers is an analogy for the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)."
Because it is partially realized through the three contemplations, it is said that "one sees but little"; even those in the tenth stage of the Separate Teaching have not yet been able to see [it].
Next, the commentary explains the title:
"The Golden Scalpel of the Perfect *Ī* is used to pierce the cataracts of ignorance of the four eyes, so that everywhere one may see Vairocana."

The finger pointing at Buddha-nature is partial and expedient; it fragments doubt by employing the firm, and uses dreams to entrust to guests, establishing host and guest so that observers may exercise forbearance.

Regarding terms such as "Yuan" (圓) and "I" (伊), "Yuan-I" refers to the *Jinpi* (Golden Scalpel), which employs analogies for the teaching of the Three Virtues; "Xi-fang-I" (Western I) refers to the same.

The characters are like the legs of a cauldron, yet they still have accompanying threads; this can be compared to the meaning of the three virtues of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) being neither vertical nor horizontal.
This principle extends through the six stages of realization (liu ji). Because seeing the revealed truth is called the Buddha-eye, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states:

"One who studies the Mahāyāna, though possessing only the physical eye, is said to possess the Buddha-eye; those who are deluded regarding this principle and teaching are said to possess the other four eyes."

Although afflictions and delusions are numerous, they are all subsumed within ignorance (*avidyā*). While the four eyes perceive distinctions, these arise due to the ignorance that shares the same essence [as the Buddha-nature].

By using the surgical lancet of the Vajra teaching, one excises the ignorance of the four eyes, causing them to return to the nature of the Buddha-eye’s seed-wisdom (*jñāna*); since there is no phenomenon external to this nature, it is said that "all is seen.

To shatter the biased attachments of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, the name "Vajra" is established; because it transcends the four extremes and is free from the hundred [delusions], it is called a "dream."

To indicate that his mind wanders beyond the principles [of conventional doctrine], he established a pseudonym as a "guest"; since he resolves doubts regarding the nature of conditions (*pratyaya*), he is designated as the "host.
Next, the entry into the text for explanation is divided into three parts: first, the introductory section; second, from "Formerly... onwards, the main body;

and third, from "At this time... onwards, the dissemination section. The first part [the introduction] is further divided into two: first, humbling oneself and stating one's intent; within this, first, humbling oneself.
The Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànrán has, since he first unworthily partook of the Buddhist scriptures many years ago, never ceased to keep the meaning of *buddhatā* (foxing) in his heart.
"Cháng" means "formerly"; "yóu" is used as a particle. ○ Next, the statement of intent.
I fear that those who do not understand this will practice asceticism. There are two meanings to this:

first, they are deluded regarding themselves, for what reason would they take the *Buddhadhātu-sūtra* (Scripture on Buddha-nature) to heart as the foundation of the myriad practices? Second, regarding others:
if both self and others do not understand, their concurrent practice is irrational; such a seal [of understanding] is identical to that of demons and externalists. Therefore, it is said:
"Empty for those who are merely empty" means it is void. ○ Next, the correct elucidation of its functional capacity has two parts: first, a general explanation of Buddha-nature.
This great teaching is established because its efficacy lies herein;
it is called "great" because it reveals that which the civil teachings rely upon. ○ Second, the explanation of it being the ultimate destination of all phenomena.
First, by simultaneously presenting both the Dharma and its parable, it clarifies the destination of the practice of cultivation.
This is the common path for the ten thousand streams, the ultimate convergence of all currents, the great purport of all dharmas, and that which practitioners aspire to attain.
Next, the tenets of our own and other schools are shown:
if one contemplates this by relying upon such reflection, then ordinary and sagely beings are of one suchness; form and fragrance are extinguished into purity;

and even the *ābhāsvara* (Avīci) realm, including both its environment and its inhabitants, is entirely contained within the self-mind of the ultimate Sage. The body and land of Vairocana do not transcend a single thought-moment of an ordinary person.

Because the essence of the three thousand worlds within the hundred realms is fully present, it is said that even in the Avīci hell, where both the environment and its inhabitants are entirely present, the self-mind of the ultimate Sage still remains there.
It is not only that ordinary beings reside within the ultimate Sage; the ultimate Sage likewise resides within ordinary beings. Question:

Since ordinary beings possess the nature of the Sage, what is the nature of that nature when they are being burned and boiled in Avīci? Answer: From the perspective of phenomena, it exists due to delusion.

Regarding burning and non-burning, from the perspective of principle and awakening, there is neither burning nor non-burning. If this is so, since both the ordinary and the base equally possess the nature in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), how can one answer that "the nature is pervasive"?
To say that the nature is pervasive refers to the nature of principle (*li*). Because it is the nature within the realm of awakened wisdom, it is called Buddha-nature.
Just as the nature of fire pervades bamboo and wood, even when the bamboo and wood are split or broken, how does this harm the nature of fire? It continues to burn and cook all things.
The nature of birth is inherently free from decay and affliction; if this is so, how can the nature of birth and the Buddha-nature be identical?
Answer: The nature of wood and the nature of fire are fundamentally identical. When water flows through bamboo or wood, the nature of fire remains distinct and clear without being lost or diminished.

Because the principle resides within the phenomenon, it receives the names of "ordinary" or "inferior," such as being burned or boiled; if the phenomenon were entirely absent, [the name would not apply].

Question: What is the principle here? If that were so, why does the discourse on *nirvāṇa* address its nature in relation to birth? Answer: It is because one fears that [discussing] its nature directly might give rise to confusion;
therefore, it is discussed in relation to realization and in terms of principle. For example, in empty space there is no phenomenon external to it. Question:
If that were so, would it only burn sentient beings and not burn the Buddha-nature? Answer: When it burns sentient beings, what is the essence of that [sentient being]? Answer: Its essential nature.
Its form is like empty space; when heated, there is no actual time of burning. Upon reaching the state of burning, burning itself is non-burning.
Following the nature of phenomena that undergoes burning, one accords with the principle of conditions without loss or disappearance. It is like a person binding a thief:

the binding of the evil body and mind does not affect the good nature of the mind, which fundamentally remains unbound. Binding is merely a hollow contrivance. If one clings to this binding, the mind wanders to the limits of heaven.

Next, the main body of the teaching has two parts. △ First, the essence of the true cause pervades all four [categories]. 4. First, that insentient things possess the Buddha-nature, in three sections.
First, the question and answer. 2. First, the reason for posing the question:
Having long contemplated this during a quiet night, my reflections remained unceasing; suddenly, as if falling asleep, I was not yet awake. I said:
Sentient beings without consciousness possess Buddha-nature.

As for the mention of "tranquil night" and so forth: it means that one realizes phenomena are nothing but nature, which is tranquil; yet because ignorance remains entirely present, it is called "night.

Having accumulated this contemplation for a long time, one contemplates the principle and takes pity on sentient beings, not calculating the reality of their nature—just as when one has fallen asleep, one speaks of the true reality as if it were real.

Because the substance of marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is quiescent, it is called "non-awakening. ○ Next, the actual presentation of the dialogue has two parts: first, the question; second, [the answer]. First, the question has two parts:
first, the general heading indicating the name of the person asking the question.
Furthermore, while asleep in a dream, he suddenly sees a man who says, "I am a rustic guest."
Next, the outward appearance of the one being represented is described:

his demeanor was coarse and rugged, and his movements were inconsistent. Standing flat-footed before [the Master], he said to him, "Just now I suddenly heard that insentient things possess Buddha-nature;
was this something you, Venerable Sir, have expounded?"

Coarse and unruly expressions manifest a mind that wanders outside of principle; they do not constantly manifest through body or speech, but are negligent and intrusive, standing level with those before them to express self-reliance and contempt for others. Next, he briefly answers:
"It is so," the other says.
△ Second, the question-and-answer section has two parts. First, an objection based on the provisional text concerning *nirvāṇa*. The guest said:

"I, your servant, have humbly sought the Buddhist teachings and briefly investigated their source. When this doctrine is extensively expounded, how could it surpass the final, ultimate proclamation of the Buddha at the twin śāla trees?
Yet you say that Buddha-nature does not apply to insentient things; why do you alone claim they are devoid of it?"
"Does emotion possess a nature?
Next, the response to the second [question] begins by citing the ancients to concede and then refute [the objection].
I said: "The ancients even claimed that icchantikas exist; it is not at all surprising that they would say insentient things do not exist."
Next, I shall cite the authentic teachings to demonstrate this.

However, as the teachings are divided into the Great and Small Vehicles, their statements differ significantly. If one says that insentient things are [sentient], one should not say they possess nature;
if one says they possess nature, it would be inconsistent to call them insentient.

"Vast" means great. As for the phrase "if one says they are equal," this refers to the mutual sublation of delusion and awakening. From the perspective of delusion and following phenomena, what nature can there be in either the sentient or the insentient?
From the perspective of awakening and following principle, the sentient and the insentient are identical as one; who then can distinguish between them?

To further calculate based on the distinction between the sentient and the insentient is why it is said that they do not accord. △ Third, the question and answer, in two parts: first, the re-examination.
The guest asked: "Why are the *Nirvāṇa* section and the *Mahāyāna* section listed side by side?
Since the *Nirvāṇa* section belongs to the Mahāyāna, why does it also clarify that walls and such are not of a [substantial] nature? Next, the second part of the reply consists of two sections:
first, stating the intention and providing a general refutation.

I replied: "Because you were not conversant with the Buddha-nature, nor with the distinctions between the progressive and regressive teachings, nor between the provisional and the ultimate, you have come to doubt this as if it were the same as the common person's view.

I shall now provide you with a detailed citation of the scriptural texts so that future generations who wish to cite this passage to prove that the Buddha-nature is not insentient may well grasp the intent of the sutras;
they will not obscure the principle of nature, and they will know that what I have established accords perfectly with the core of the scriptures."
Next, citing the scriptures in two parts: First, a general citation to demonstrate the same principle.
The present treatise establishes that the essence of the true cause (zhengyin) of sentient beings is all-pervasive; the scriptural passages cited here all employ empty space as a metaphor for it.
Second, the specific citations in two parts: First, citing the Buddha’s teachings to show their agreement with the true cause.
Therefore, the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, chapter thirty-one, states: "The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like space; it is neither internal nor external.
If it were either internal or external, how could it be said to exist everywhere? Please observe the single character "existence" (*you*): what does space not encompass?
Thus, we know that the scriptural text does not permit [the Buddha-nature] to be exclusively internal or exclusively external; hence it says "neither internal nor external," and so forth.
Furthermore, it says, "It is like space. Since it speaks of the Buddha-nature of sentient beings, how could this not be the rational nature as the primary cause?
○ Next, the clarification of Kāśyapa’s objection has two parts: first, clarifying the origin of the objection.
Next, Kāśyapa asked, "What is meant by 'being like empty space'? The Buddha then answered with the unimpeded state of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).
Is this not because the true cause and the fruit are non-dual? Since the Buddha answered Kāśyapa from the perspective of the fruit, he employed provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) to sever the fruits;
yet, as for the conditions and causes upon that fruit, all are existent. Thus, Kāśyapa raised an objection, claiming that the analogy of emptiness and the analogy of the Dharma are not equivalent.

The Tathāgata’s explanation of the powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth as being like the analogy of empty space—wherein Kāśyapa raises the objection that the fruits of the provisional teachings cannot be made equal—is concluded.
Next, the clarification of Kāśyapa’s formulation of the objection has two parts: first, the formulation of the objection itself.
Therefore, Kāśyapa asked: "If the Tathāgata’s buddha-nature and nirvāṇa are existent, then space should also be existent?
Next, the Buddha’s response is explained in two parts: first, the simultaneous presentation of two perspectives.
The Buddha first answers in accordance with the question, and subsequently reaffirms his fundamental position to clarify emptiness.
Next, he provides a dual explanation of two points: first, he explains the initial intent; second, he first cites the provisional text of the scripture, which contains three meanings.
First, he follows the question by stating: "Is it not nirvana that is spoken of as nirvana? Here, "non-nirvana" refers to conditioned phenomena and afflictions.
To say that affliction is not the Tathāgata, yet to say that the Tathāgata is not the Tathāgata, refers to the icchantikas and those of the two vehicles;
to speak of what is not Buddha-nature as being Buddha-nature, while what is not Buddha-nature refers to walls, tiles, and stones.
Next, the inquiry into the intent of the scripture’s composition concerns the provisional and the real. First, regarding the inquiry into the intent of the scripture’s composition:
we now ask, if tiles and stones are eternally non-existent, are the afflictions of the two vehicles likewise eternally non-existent?

Therefore, one knows that the scriptural text employs the teaching of skillful means to speak of the three remedies as a temporary expedient; it provisionally speaks of the three realms of existence in order to refute the three types of non-existence. Consequently, following this passage...
The conclusion states: "There is nothing in all worlds that is not empty space.

Regarding the Buddha’s intention in saying "in contrast to empty space," he takes the three—tiles, stones, and so forth—as the objects of contrast; therefore, it is said that everything is none other than the Tathāgata and the other two.
○ Next, the fourfold reiteration of the objection: First, the objection that emptiness is made into existence, which accords with the severance of provisional wisdom.
Kāśyapa again takes the four great elements as a parallel to argue that emptiness is made into existence; thus Kāśyapa says: "In the world, there is nothing that is not the four great elements.
Since the four great elements are 'existence' and empty space is 'non-existence,' why is the latter not also called 'existence'? This is the intention of Kāśyapa.
Because emptiness is non-obstructive, it is the greatest of all existents.
When it was first said that "the world also does not exist," Kāśyapa perceived that the Buddha stood in contrast to the great void;
he regarded the emptiness of the world and the emptiness of the four great elements as the objects of contrast, while the emptiness of the great void was the singular Great One.

Taking emptiness as that which can oppose and that which is opposed: it is precisely because there is that which can oppose that it is said, "In the world, there is also nothing [that opposes it]," and so forth.

"The world" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); these are empty. That which is not the four great elements is the Great Empty Space (*mahākāśa*). Below the section on the four great elements, all four great elements are phenomena that possess opposition (*sapratigha*).
When they oppose emptiness, they are also called the "Great Empty Element. The essence of space has no opposition; it is that which opposes the four great elements.

It should be called "existent" (*sat*); thus the concluding passage states: "Because emptiness has no counterpart, it is the greatness of existence. For example, although the primary cause is likened to empty space, emptiness is not a mere non-existence;
this may likewise be applied to the provisional, the conditional, and the understanding [aspects of the threefold truth], which are termed "existent.
Within the four types of emptiness mentioned in the text, the first two lines cite the four great elements established by the Buddha, while the latter two lines present a twofold critique of both.

"Why is it not called 'existence'? Regarding the first intention behind this: it is not that the Great [Elements] are made to face the Great so as to cause the world to be non-existent (for "non-Great" is itself the Great, and the void world is itself the Four Great Elements). Regarding the second intention: because the Four Great Elements possess the void, and since there is a counterpart for every counterpart of the Great, why is it not called "existence"?
The remaining two points are as stated in the text. Second, the Buddha’s compliant response.

After this, the Buddha abandons the analogy and proceeds from the Dharma to explain extensively that *nirvāṇa* is not the same as empty space; if *nirvāṇa* is not the same as the other two [space and consciousness], it is also different from them.
Third, he cites the preceding [arguments] to resolve the difficulty and bring the meaning back to the ultimate reality.
Therefore, we know that the Sūtra concludes the argument with the "correct cause" (samyag-hetu) by asking what in all the world is not subsumed;
how could it exclude afflictions or those of the two vehicles? What does the term "empty space" (ākāśa) not encompass? Why then would it reject walls, tiles, stones, and the like?
Fourth, distinguishing the true direct cause from the provisional conditions and understanding:

The Buddha later further stated that although emptiness and nirvana are both not subsumed within the mundane world, nirvana and the Tathāgata possess realization and vision, whereas empty space is merely eternal;
therefore, [the former] is not so. Is this not precisely the difference between the direct cause and the conditions and understanding?

The Tathāgata’s Nirvāṇa, which is taught through provisional means as the ever-abiding conditions and causes within empty space, is distinct [from other views] because it is the true principle of the direct cause (*samyag-hetu*).
○ Next, the second section establishes the correct doctrine in three parts: first, exposing false emptiness to refute externalist calculations; first, stating the purpose for introducing this.

Next, the Buddha returns to his central thesis to clarify that emptiness is not a form of existence; fearing that people of the world might mistakenly take a false conception of emptiness to be the Buddha-nature, he further employs ten successive arguments to refute such errors.
Next, the explicit clarification of the "perversion of emptiness" consists of ten sections. △ First, the refutation of mental factors (*caitta*). The first section states:
"Worldly people say that 'empty space' is formless, non-obstructive, and invisible. The Buddha says: 'This is actually a mental factor, subsumed within the three periods of time;
because its description resembles a mental factor, the Buddha refutes it. [The opponent asks: 'What do worldly people mean by "within the body"? "

Regarding the mental factors (*caitta*) of the distinct mind: those that initially resemble speech and so forth are like non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) because they lack color and form; thus, they are among the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Each passage states that "worldly speech" refers to the refutation of the biased attachment [to the view] that sentient beings are the Buddha-nature.
2. Refuting Luminosity. Furthermore, the non-Buddhists say that space is luminosity.
The Buddha says: "That too is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*). What is different about what is said by the world regarding the interior of the body from a material phenomenon?"
The second [view] conceives emptiness as being luminosity. △ Third, the refutation of the dwelling place:
Some say that the dwelling place refers to what is spoken of in the world as "within the body"; is this not a dwelling place?
The third [view] conceives emptiness as abiding in a place of emptiness. △ Fourth, the refutation of the sequence.
Some say that regarding the sequence of time, within the body it must necessarily follow the movement of each moment (*kṣaṇa*).

The fourth [point] considers the sequence of emptiness to be unconfused; therefore, by citing the *kṣaṇa*—wherein things perish as they arise and become empty as they perish—it refutes worldly attachments.
△ Fifth, the refutation of the three locations.
Some say that one does not depart from three dharmas: first, emptiness; second, reality; and third, both emptiness and reality. The Buddha said:

"If one speaks of emptiness, it is because there is nothing in a particular place. If one speaks of reality, it is because there is nothing in the place of emptiness. If one speaks of both emptiness and reality, it is because there is nothing in both places.
The world says that even within the body there are still deficiencies, yet they calculate emptiness and both together as being external.
The fifth set of three dharmas consists of: first, reckoning the empty place as empty; second, reckoning the substantial place as empty;
third, reckoning both together as empty. △ Sixth, the refutation of that which is conditioned.

Some say that the method of action (*kriyā*) is like the worldly expression "the body has perished" when applied to a house; thus, it corresponds to the true nature (*dharmatā*) and is identical to the method of action.

Regarding the sixth point, the "method of action of removal": this refers to the category of emptying a space by removing objects, as it is similar to the act of construction; therefore, the example of "removing a house" is used to explain it.
△ Seventh, the refutation of the unobstructed locus (*anāvṛta-sthāna*).

Some say that where there is no obstruction, the Buddha said there is a portion and there is a constituent. If it possesses all portions, then because it does not exist in other places, worldly convention says that within the body, it does not exist in other locations.
When the seventh [consciousness] speaks of "where there is no obstruction," it reveals that there is a location where space is absent. As for saying "there is a portion" and "there is a constituent":
For example, the emptiness within the interior of the body-house is called "partial emptiness" (fen-kong), while the great void of space is "complete emptiness" (ju-kong).
△ Eighth, the refutation of [the claim that] conjunction exists alongside existence.
Some say that conjunction exists alongside existence; the Buddha stated that there are three kinds of conjunction: first, like a bird alighting on a tree; second, like a sheep... [text fragment].
Regarding the three cases of mutual contact, they are like the two fingers already joined; the worldly expression "within the body" refers to the joining of the two fingers.

As for the eighth statement regarding "conjunction with existence," this refers to the conjunction of space with existence. Therefore, the Buddha raised these three points to challenge [the opponent's position].
Although all are cases of conjunction, the meanings of conjunction differ, and thus their own positions collapse. In the first case, one moves while the other does not.
When the second [finger] moves, both move; when the third moves, both remain still.
This is precisely because there is space within the boundaries that the two fingers are able to join together. △ Ninth, the refutation of the vessel.
Some say: "It is like the emptiness within a vessel; what is different about the interior of the body from the emptiness within a vessel?
This is the ninth point of visibility. Tenth, the refutation of the location indicated:
Some say, "As for the place pointed out by the Buddha, he said it possesses spatial dimensions; surely the interior of the body must also possess spatial dimensions."
Regarding "the space at the tip of the tenth finger": this refers to the space following the direction of the finger; it does not mean that some other specific thing is empty.

III. Conclusion. The Buddha concludes by stating: because all things arising from causes and conditions are impermanent, these ten erroneous conceptions regarding space as being non-Buddha-nature are impermanent, for they are subsumed within the three periods of time.
As stated in the text. Next, the conclusion indicates the true emptiness:

"Empty space differs from that [conditioned phenomena] as it pervades all places. This responds to Kāśyapa’s question and reaffirms the fundamental principle by using the metaphor of empty space to illustrate the True Cause (the Buddha-nature).
As in the text. ○ Third, the conclusion and reprimand of the five [errors]: First, the reprimand for equating [the Buddha’s teaching] with false emptiness.
Why do people of the world abandon the Buddha’s true teaching to align themselves with false emptiness?
○ Next, the reprimand for using provisional fruits, conditions, and knowledge to challenge the true causes and fruits of the true cause.

How can one use the fact that the fruits of wisdom (*jñāna*) and cessation (*prahāṇa*) possess the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the condition of knowledge (*vidya-pratyaya*) to challenge the primary cause [of Buddhahood]?
Since the Tathāgata is the fruit of wisdom and *nirvāṇa* is the fruit of cessation, these fruits of wisdom and cessation possess the nature of the object-condition and the condition of knowledge;
therefore, Kāśyapa challenges [the Buddha], saying: "The Tathāgata, the Buddha-nature, and *nirvāṇa* exist."
Third, the explanation of the citations and their intended meaning:

Since worldly people frequently cite the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* to raise objections, this text quotes it extensively to silence further debate. However, you [the opponent] have not seen the passages concerning *nirvāṇa*;
your empty imitation of worldly people’s use of tiles and stones as obstacles is difficult to justify and is entirely inconsistent with the correct principle.
This is precisely because the disciple does not know whether the Buddha-nature advances or regresses.

this refers to how the primary cause—the Middle Way—serves as the object for those who rely on the teaching path of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) to ascend to the stages (*bhūmi*).

Because the first and last [stages] are termed the "limited nature of the principle," one knows that the nature of the *dharmatā* does not pervade insentient things—this is the meaning of the distinction.

Therefore, in the provisional teachings, those at the stage of ordinary beings should hear the doctrine that insentient things lack nature; it is not said that the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment) possesses nature.
In accordance with their mental calculations, it is said that there is nothing to be removed; this absence of inherent nature is itself Buddha-nature.
Next, [the Master] Far (Daoyuan) extensively cites a period [of teaching] to reveal the reason for establishing provisional means within the Nirvana Sutra, thereby judging and refuting deluded minds.

Furthermore, throughout his entire lifetime, he has already extensively manifested the sudden [teaching], such as in the *Avataṃsaka*, where the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual, Samantabhadra and the Universal Eye are undifferentiated by the three, and in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, where all defiled and pure phenomena are mutually integrated; in the *Vimalakīrti*, where inconceivable pores contain all things;

in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, where the net-like radiance of light is nothing other than the Dharma-realm; and in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, where all dharmas are blended together as non-dual. This is the fundamental [nature].

The ultimate reality of all phenomena is identical to *nirvāṇa*; it merely prevents the deluded attachments of the provisional and the final, thereby distinguishing the correct conditions and causes and pointing toward the general direction.

If one clings to the real, one is confused about the provisional and loses even the real; if one clings to the provisional while being confused about the real, then both the provisional and the real are lost.
Examining the disciples, they are still ignorant of the Lesser Vehicle because their minds are dark regarding the Great Teaching; outside of the mind, there are no objects.
If there are no objects external to the mind, then insentient things would lack their own nature; if there are objects external to the mind, then this is not the Great Teaching.

The Great Teaching holds that both the primary and secondary worlds, as well as defilement and purity, are solely mind. By observing the mind through the mind and observing the environment through the mind, these two are non-dual. To discard insentient things separately from the mind is erroneous.

Thirteenth: Mind and matter are non-dual; they are simply both "only. Just as water is only water and ice is only ice, these two have no dual substance—they are one substance, which is the totality of mind.

Eighteenth: The three causes for the virtuous qualities of the nature of sentient beings are fully present;

"Thank you," the forest guest said, his heart filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy. "To cast away one's body cannot repay this kindness; to grind one's bones to powder would hardly suffice as recompense. I shall only do this:

Regarding the first section: because one grieves over what was not heard in the past and rejoices at having realized it now, it is said that [the feelings] "converge.

I replied: "The Buddha has sincere admonitions that may serve as a standard. A sutra says: 'If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings would remain submerged in suffering;

In the end, one will surely obtain benefit, just as a person who has fallen to the ground rises from that very ground. One should exercise great compassion and not cause others distress.

For example, when the Bodhisattva Nandiyashas preached to a layperson that the essence of desire is itself the nature of the Path, he was slandered by Abhimāna, who then enacted a formal act of banishment against him.
Nandiyashas, knowing that [the slanderer] would immediately receive retribution in this very life, forcibly preached the Great Dharma to him.
The workings of poison are such that they plant the seeds for hearing the Dharma over a long period; the case of the fourfold assembly is likewise.

Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is cited as proof: "falling to the ground" is a metaphor for falling into the realms of suffering due to slander, while "rising" is a metaphor for the distant benefit [of future awakening]. ○ Fourth, the conclusion.
You should proceed with composure, observing whether the timing is favorable for advancement or not, protecting the other's feelings while conforming to the Buddha’s original intent.

Nature. ○ Next, it is shown that the substance and magnitude of these three causes are both all-pervasive.

The Buddhas are equal to the Dharma-realm.

Having already established that faith is pervasive, we next demonstrate that it is pervasively complete.

Since it is identical to all Buddhas in being equal to the *dharmadhātu*, this nature of pervasiveness is fully endowed with the bodies of all Buddhas. One body is all bodies, just as the lands manifested by all Buddhas are one land and all lands.

If worldly people say that sentient beings possess only the nature of purity, and that the cultivation of the myriad practices constitutes the substance of their functional effort; ... [text continues] ... [The text continues with the subsequent sections of the commentary.]

I do not understand the initial meaning. Second, there is doubt that the three causes of the nature [of Buddhahood] are not coextensive with the three bodies.

Why? Because if the Reward-body and Transformation-body are excluded, it remains merely a sentient being.
They do not understand the subsequent meaning. Third, regarding the nature of doubt: they claim that the three causal natures do not possess the essence of the three bodies or the three virtues.

The direct cause is the Dharma Jewel; the immediate cause is the Buddha Jewel; and the contributory cause is the Sangha Jewel.

Because the Buddha-nature is non-dual, it is said to be of one essence (*ekatva*). The essence of awakening and cognition is the essence of Buddha-nature; the essence free from defilement is the essence of Dharma-nature; and the essence free from contention is the Sangha.
These Three Jewels are endowed with the three thousand realms of the hundred worlds; these three thousand realms of the hundred worlds are exclusively the Perfect [Teaching].
The essence of Buddha-nature is eternally present and is not something created by external things; it is called the realm of non-action.

This "realm" refers to the Four Noble Truths and the three thousand realms within the ten dharma-realms. Birth-and-death is itself suffering; realizing that birth-and-death is itself nirvana is what is meant by the vow:
"I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings. The three thousand realms within the ten dharma-realms fully possess the three delusions; realizing that these afflictions are themselves bodhi.
The afflictions are innumerable, yet I vow to sever them; birth and death are themselves nirvana, and I vow to realize the perfect Buddha-nature, which is the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
Delusion is itself bodhi, and there is nothing that is not prajñā; this is the inexhaustible Dharma-gate, and I vow to know it.
Delusion and wisdom are non-dual, and the bodies of sentient beings and Buddhas are identical; suffering and its origin are but the mind. Thus, the Four Great Vows encompass and harmonize all.

"One is all"—this statement has its evidence. The arousal of the mind through the nature of conditions encompasses both the extraction [of suffering] and the inclusion [of joy], transcending the partial and the small;

If there are those who are heedless regarding the teaching and give rise to contention, one should say to them: "Hearing [this teaching] has already established the seeds [of Buddhahood]; we dare not disparage you.

Second, citing texts to harmonize disputes:

Even the followers of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas cannot fathom them, let alone ordinary worldlings who wish to judge this matter. It is like [the case of] a living being..."
